engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Rating Progress Reality
chess.body: 800→1000: Learn not to blunder pieces for free. 1000→1200: Basic tactics (forks, pins). 1200→1500: Strategy (plans, pawn structure). 1500→1800: Calculation depth + endgames. 1800+: Opening theory + deep calculation. Most adults plateau at 1000-1200 because they skip tactics training. Do 10 puzzles daily — minimum. No shortcut.

book.author: Annie Duke
book.chapter: Resulting: Don't Judge Decisions by Outcomes
book.lesson: Professional poker player Annie Duke's core insight: we judge decisions by outcomes (resulting), but the quality of a decision is independent of its outcome. A bad decision can produce a good outcome (lucky). A good decision can produce a bad outcome (unlucky). If you judge your decisions by results, you'll reinforce bad thinking when it gets lucky and abandon good thinking when it gets unlucky. The fix: evaluate decisions by the quality of the reasoning and information available at the time, not by what happened. This is how professional investors, poker players, and military strategists think.
book.key_quote: A great decision made with the information available can still produce a bad outcome. That doesn't make it a bad decision.
book.action: Review your last 3 major decisions. For each one, ask: was this a good decision given what I knew? Separate the quality of the process from the result.
crux: Every decision is a bet on an uncertain future. Certainty is not available.
Outcome ≠ decision quality. Chess is nearly all skill; life is poker — skill plus luck.
'Resulting' is judging a decision by how it turned out. It is the core error.
Replace true/false with a confidence percentage. 'I'm 70% on this' is honest and updatable.
Saying 'I'm not sure' is a strength. Pretended certainty blocks learning.
Beliefs are formed first and vetted later, if ever. Assume yours are unaudited.
Motivated reasoning: contradicting evidence gets scrutinised, confirming evidence gets waved through.
Self-serving bias: wins are skill, losses are luck. This makes experience useless.
Build a truth-seeking group with an explicit charter: accuracy over comfort, dissent welcomed.
Argue the other side properly. Steelman it, don't strawman it.
Separate signal from noise in feedback. A small sample tells you almost nothing.
Use temporal distance — 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years — before deciding under emotion.
Backcast from success and pre-mortem from failure. Both, not one.
Tilt is real. Recognise the emotional state and stop deciding while in it.
learnings: A good decision can lose. A bad decision can win. Track process, not scoreboard.
Confidence expressed as a percentage is falsifiable. Confidence expressed as certainty is not.
Without separating luck from skill, ten years of experience teaches nothing.
You need people who will tell you that you were wrong.
examples: Pete Carroll's Super Bowl XLIX pass call was widely branded the worst in history. The interception rate on that play was about 2% — the decision was defensible, the outcome was not.
Duke won $4m at poker by focusing on decision quality across thousands of hands rather than the result of any single one.
In 1979, near-universal belief that Nixon's tapes would exonerate him did not survive contact with the tapes. Consensus is not evidence.
adapt: Log every trade with the thesis and a confidence %, not just entry and exit. The ledger is the point.
45.8% win rate at +0.171R is a good system. Judge it on 459 trades, not on last week.
After a losing trade, ask what a repeat of that decision returns over 100 tries. Usually the answer is 'fine'.
The 50% real win rate on the signals feed is the honest number. Publish that, not the flattering one.

father.title: Let her struggle briefly
father.do: When a toy is just out of reach, wait five seconds before helping.
father.why: Effort tolerance is trainable. Instant rescue is comfortable for you and teaches her that difficulty is someone else's problem.

father.why: Competence gaps between parents are self-reinforcing — the more skilled parent does more, and the gap widens. Deliberately absorbing the early incompetence is how it closes.

interview_tech.q: How does IFRS 16 change the picture for a retailer with 60 leases?
interview_tech.a: Operating leases come on balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Rent expense is replaced by depreciation plus interest, so EBITDA rises — often materially for retail — while EBIT moves little. Interest is front-loaded, so early-life leases depress net income versus the old treatment. Watch three consequences: gearing ratios jump and can breach covenants written pre-IFRS 16; EBITDA-based multiples are no longer comparable to history; and store-level return metrics need restating or you will misjudge performance.

interview_tech.q: Explain working capital optimisation to a non-finance retail board.
interview_tech.a: Working capital is cash tied up in running the business — stock on shelves and money owed to you, less money you owe suppliers. Every day of stock is cash sitting in a warehouse instead of in the bank. Frame it in days and rupees, not ratios: 'we hold 95 days of stock; every day we cut releases AED 1.1M in cash we can spend on new stores instead of borrowing.' Boards act on that. They do not act on 'DIO improved 4%.'

interview_soft.q: What is your biggest professional failure?
interview_soft.a: Pick a real one with a number, not a disguised strength. The structure: what you owned, what specifically you got wrong, what it cost, what you changed in your process, and evidence the change held. The disqualifying answers are 'I work too hard' and any failure where the fault lands on someone else. If you cannot name the cost in money or time, it was not a real failure and they will know.

interview_soft.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
interview_soft.a: Answer the real question: are you a flight risk and do you understand the ladder. Be specific about the next rung rather than the summit — 'Financial Controller for a multi-market group, then Finance Director with commercial ownership, then CFO. What I need in between is treasury depth and a full M&A cycle, which is part of why this role interests me.' Naming what you lack reads as self-aware, not weak.

cfo_field.q: The controller who never leaves the close never becomes CFO.
cfo_field.a: The job you are promoted out of is 'the person who produces the numbers'. The job you are promoted into is 'the person who decides what to do about them'. If your calendar is 70% close, reconciliation and audit prep, you are demonstrating that you are excellent at the job you already have. Push the close down: a well-run retail group closes in 5 working days, and every day you shave buys back roughly 12 days a year of capacity to spend on decisions instead of production.

cfo_field.q: The Gulf pays for scarcity, not for years.
cfo_field.a: Salary in the region tracks the intersection of skills, not the length of the CV. CA plus genuine FP&A plus retail plus a system implementation is a much rarer combination than any one of them is deep. If you are negotiating, the leverage is in naming the intersection, not in listing the years. And check the structure: basic versus allowances changes gratuity, which is calculated on basic salary alone.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early central control: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, avoid 3...Nf6?; instead play 3...Nd7 or 3...Nc6, then develop bishop to g4 or e7, castle quickly, and prevent White’s rapid d4‑c3‑Qb3 attack that won you the game.Your main flaw was passive, cramped development—after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 you let White seize the center with d4 and c3, then attack your queen. Switch to a more active Philidor: play 3…Nd7 (or 3…Nc6), develop the bishop to g4 or e7, castle early, and challenge White’s center with …exd4 or …c5. This solidifies your position and prevents the quick collapse you suffered.
lichess_games.standout: Over in 17 moves — decided in the opening, so the opening is what to study.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your opening choices are leaving you defenseless—every game you play you’re already a step behind, and the stats prove it. Stop relying on vague “standard” lines and drill the most common traps in the Sicilian and King's Indian; you must recognize the first 6‑8 moves and have a concrete plan before move 4. Play three full‑length games a day against 1500‑1600 opponents, pause after every loss to write down the exact move where you first deviated, and replay the position with a stronger engine until you can see the winning continuation—repeat until you can’t lose the same line twice.
